name: Hack2hire
tagline: Interview prep platform built around real technical interview questions and mock interviews for big tech hiring loops.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely build you a drilling app: editor, timer, hidden test cases, spaced repetition, even an LLM that critiques your solution and your explanation. What it cannot build is the reason people pay, which is knowing which questions actually get asked, in which loop, at which company, this quarter. That intel comes from people who just sat the interview and reported back, and from human mock interviewers who have run the real thing. Your local build starts as an empty database and stays empty until you fill it, and if you already knew the questions you would not need the product. Build the trainer, buy the corpus, or accept that you are practicing on whatever you happened to remember.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you store interview problems, solve them in a timed editor against hidden test cases, get LLM feedback on solution and explanation, and resurface weak ones on a spaced repetition schedule.
requirements: Your own list of problems and test cases, typed in or imported
An OpenAI-compatible API key in .env if you want feedback and grading
whatYouLose: The curated bank of company-specific, recently-asked questions, which is the entire point
Live mock interviews with humans who have actually conducted the loop
Any signal about what a hiring bar looks like beyond your own guessing
Editorial solutions, follow-up variants and interviewer-perspective notes
Other candidates grinding the same set to compare against
moatNotes: The corpus decays fast, which is also why it is hard to copy: it needs a steady stream of fresh candidate reports to stay worth anything.
whyPeopleStillPay: People do not pay for a code editor with a timer, they pay to reduce variance on a decision worth tens of thousands of dollars a year. Paying for question intel and a mock interview with someone who has run the loop is cheap insurance against a bad forty-five minutes, and the anxiety of the job hunt makes it feel cheaper still. A self-built trainer helps you practice, but it cannot tell you what to practice, and that gap is the whole business.
notes: The trainer is a weekend; the question bank is not. The moat is a stream of fresh candidate reports plus humans who have sat on the other side of the table.
prompt:
Build a local-only technical interview trainer as a single Next.js 15 app (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind). No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Storage: SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/trainer.db, schema created on boot. Tables: problems (id, title, company, role, tags, difficulty, prompt_markdown, starter_code, reference_solution, created_at), tests (id, problem_id, input_json, expected_json, hidden boolean), attempts (id, problem_id, code, language, elapsed_seconds, passed_count, failed_count, self_rating, llm_feedback, created_at), reviews (problem_id, due_on, interval_days, ease).

Pages:
- /problems : list with filters by company, tag, difficulty, and a "due today" filter.
- /problems/new : form to add a problem plus test cases, and a JSON import box that accepts an array of problems so a bank can be pasted in bulk.
- /solve/[id] : split view. Left is the problem markdown. Right is a Monaco editor with the starter code. A visible countdown timer starting at 35 minutes, plus a "clock only, no pause" mode. Buttons: Run visible tests, Submit (runs all tests including hidden).
- /review : today's queue, ordered by due_on.
- /stats : attempts over time, pass rate by tag, median time to first passing submission.

Execution: JavaScript solutions only. Run submitted code in a Node child process with a 5 second timeout and no network, passing each test input as JSON on stdin and comparing parsed stdout to expected. Kill and report on timeout. Do not attempt a real sandbox and say so in the README.

LLM feedback: optional. If OPENAI_API_KEY is set in .env, after submit send the problem prompt, the code and the test results to a chat completion and ask for: correctness notes, complexity analysis, and two follow-up questions an interviewer would ask. Store the response on the attempt. If the key is absent, hide the feature cleanly instead of erroring.

Spaced repetition: on submit, ask the user to self-rate 1-4. Update interval_days with a simple SM-2 style schedule and set due_on.

Out of scope: Python or C++ execution, multiplayer, mock interview video, any bundled question content. Ship the database empty and put a five-problem example JSON in ./examples so the import path is testable.

Deliver: README with setup, .env.example with OPENAI_API_KEY, npm run dev working on a clean checkout.
